message.content: Thank you. You look pale and deeply jaundiced, but your vital signs are fairly stable. I have two questions. First, have you had any abdominal pain, itching, or weight loss in recent weeks? Second, have you vomited blood, had black tarry stools, or taken any new medications, such as NSAIDs, or drunk alcohol? I'll use your answers to decide which tests to order.

I haven't had any belly pain. As for itching and weight loss, I don't remember anything about those. The main thing is that my skin and eyes have been getting more yellow over the last four days. My stools have also been dark during that time. I haven't noticed any bleeding, and I haven't vomited blood. I've been very tired and lightheaded. I started a new cancer treatment, pembrolizumab, through an IV about two weeks ago. I don't know of any other new medicines, and I wasn't asked about NSAIDs or alcohol before, so I can't say about those.

Your symptoms began about two weeks after your first pembrolizumab dose. Pembrolizumab can make the immune system attack the liver or the red blood cells. Attacks on red blood cells cause hemolysis, which means they break down faster than the body can replace them. That can produce yellow skin, paleness and lightheadedness. Bleeding or a bile duct blockage is less likely, but I haven't ruled it out. I'm ordering blood tests to separate these causes. They cover your blood count, signs of red cell breakdown, a Coombs test, liver tests and clotting, plus a look at your blood cells under the microscope.

message.content:
The tests show your red blood cells are being destroyed by your own immune system. This is called autoimmune hemolytic anemia. LDH is very high, haptoglobin is undetectable, and the blood film shows spherocytes and young red cells. The Coombs test is strongly positive for IgG and complement. This explains the yellow skin and eyes, paleness, tiredness and lightheadedness. It most likely comes from pembrolizumab, which can trigger this immune reaction. Bleeding and a bile duct blockage are unlikely. The usual treatment is to stop pembrolizumab and start corticosteroids. You would also take folate and have a transfusion if your hemoglobin falls too low. If steroids don't work, second-line options include rituximab or IVIG. Your oncology team should be involved, and you should be admitted for monitoring.

Final diagnosis: immune checkpoint inhibitor (pembrolizumab)-induced warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, with a DAT positive for IgG and C3d.

Okay, thank you for explaining all that, doctor. So my own immune system is attacking my red blood cells, and it's probably from the pembrolizumab. That makes sense with how yellow, tired and lightheaded I've been. I understand the plan is to stop the pembrolizumab, start steroids and folate, and give a transfusion if my blood count drops too low. I'm also fine with being admitted so you can monitor me, and with my cancer team being involved. Is there anything I should watch for while I'm in the hospital?

Good question. While you're in hospital, the team will check your blood count, hemolysis markers (LDH, bilirubin, reticulocytes) and your blood sugar and blood pressure often, because steroids can affect these. Tell the nurses or doctors right away if you notice any of the following:

- More lightheadedness, fainting, a racing heart, chest pain or shortness of breath. These can mean your hemoglobin is dropping.
- Darker (tea- or cola-colored) urine, or deepening yellow skin or eyes.
- Fever, chills or other signs of infection. Steroids lower your resistance to infection.
- Black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, or stomach pain or burning. Steroids can irritate the stomach.
- Pain, swelling or redness in a leg, or sudden chest pain or breathlessness. Hemolysis can raise the risk of blood clots.
- Confusion, severe headache, or marked mood or sleep changes.
- Extreme thirst or frequent urination, which can mean high blood sugar from the steroids.

The team will also watch for other immune side effects from pembrolizumab, such as diarrhea, rash, cough or liver problems. Please also tell them about any new symptoms that you notice.

Thank you, doctor, that's really clear. I'll tell the nurses right away if I feel more lightheaded, faint, or short of breath, or if my skin or urine gets darker. I'll also speak up about any fever or chills, black or bloody stools, stomach pain, leg swelling, or chest pain. I'll mention confusion or extreme thirst too. I don't have any of those right now apart from the tiredness, lightheadedness and yellow skin. I don't have any other questions at the moment. Thank you for explaining everything.

You're welcome. I'm admitting you now, and your oncology team will be told. Pembrolizumab will be held. You'll start steroids and folate, and you'll have a transfusion if your hemoglobin falls too low. Please tell the staff straight away if anything changes. I hope you feel better soon.
